title: Empirically valid aggregate market laws beyond the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu barrier

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a set of measurable conditions under which the behavior of households combines into reliable laws for whole markets. These conditions might concern preferences, initial holdings of goods and assets, or the distribution of those characteristics across people. The goal is to measure the conditions in a specified class of markets and use them to predict subsequent prices and quantities outside the data used to develop the model. This is a research objective; the supplied material does not establish that such laws have been achieved.

The theoretical motivation is the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu result concerning aggregate excess demand: the difference between what all consumers collectively want to buy and the resources available at a given set of prices. The supplied research attributes to the Shafer–Sonnenschein handbook summary a result that, on a compact set of strictly positive prices, essentially any continuous function satisfying homogeneity and Walras’ law can be generated by an economy. Homogeneity means that changing all nominal prices proportionately does not change excess demand; Walras’ law expresses the aggregate budget constraint. The implication attributed to the theorem is that individual rationality alone leaves considerable freedom in aggregate market behavior. The exact domain and qualifications remain subject to verification because retained source text was not supplied.

Synthesis: going beyond this barrier would mean identifying additional restrictions that real markets satisfy and demonstrating their predictive value. It would not mean overturning a mathematical theorem. The intended laws would have an explicit domain: a class of markets, an equilibrium framework, observable restrictions, and a description of how prices adjust. Their usefulness would depend on whether those restrictions can be measured before outcomes and remain informative when market conditions change.

significance.text: The supplied research contrasts the existence of competitive equilibrium under appropriate assumptions with the much stronger requirements of uniqueness, stability, and quantitative prediction. Its account of the aggregation theorem explains why ordinary individual optimization does not by itself supply all of those properties. Restrictions that were both empirically credible and predictively powerful could therefore provide a foundational connection between household behavior and aggregate market outcomes.

Conditional significance: within a validated market class, the direct benefit would be disciplined predictions of how prices and quantities respond to specified changes in resources, preferences, or other modeled conditions. Uniqueness would identify one equilibrium within the model, but would not by itself make its numerical predictions accurate. Local stability would describe behavior near that equilibrium under a specified adjustment process, rather than guarantee that every initial condition converges to it. Quantitative comparative statics would additionally require an identified model and a well-defined shock.

The research cites Kirman’s 1992 critique for the distinction between individual maximization and a representative individual that supposedly maximizes on behalf of the whole economy. Successful aggregate laws could help determine when a representative-agent approximation is useful, but would not automatically validate it. That judgment would require comparisons with heterogeneous-household models and observed responses, including responses to changes in the distribution of resources.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more credible policy counterfactuals and better inputs to economic design. Those applications require additional structure: monetary and macroeconomic regimes belong to ECO-08, while mechanisms operating under private information belong to ECO-09. Accurate price and quantity predictions also do not establish welfare rankings; those require welfare-relevant information and normative assumptions. Describing the advance as a new foundational language is an evaluative analogy for its potential reach, not evidence that it would make all economic behavior predictable.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability sought here is to move from mathematical restrictions chosen for tractability to observable restrictions that hold in real markets and substantially constrain aggregate excess demand. According to the supplied account of the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu result, individual rationality alone does not do this work. The research therefore seeks additional structure in preferences, endowments, or their population distribution. The historical theorem motivates this search, but cannot establish by itself which restrictions remain undiscovered or whether later research has already achieved part of the objective.

Synthesis of the scientific barriers: the proposed restrictions must be identifiable from observations and distinguishable from convenient assumptions that merely reproduce a sample. The aggregation method must retain the aspects of household heterogeneity and resource distribution that matter for market responses. A model must also specify which shocks it can identify and how those shocks change equilibrium outcomes. Otherwise, a unique equilibrium can coexist with inaccurate or weakly identified predictions.

Synthesis of the dynamical and practical barriers: stability requires a concrete price-adjustment process and evidence that it is relevant to the markets being studied. A proof of local stability under one process does not establish stability under another, or convergence after large disturbances. Empirical implementation must measure the proposed restrictions before the prediction period, determine when they cease to hold, and quantify uncertainty. These requirements make the objective more demanding than fitting a representative consumer or proving a theorem under assumptions that have not been checked.

current_state.text: The historical foundation identified in the supplied research is Debreu’s 1974 excess-demand theorem, presented through the 1982 Shafer–Sonnenschein handbook chapter. The attributed result permits a continuous aggregate excess-demand function satisfying homogeneity and Walras’ law to be realized by an economy on a compact positive-price set. This is a mathematical aggregation result, not an empirical demonstration that observed markets are arbitrary. Debreu’s full text was reported unavailable, and the handbook statement came from a publisher summary. No retained source texts or artifact hashes were supplied for the review, so the precise theorem statement and its qualifications were not independently checked there.

Kirman’s 1992 article is cited for the methodological argument that an aggregate of individually maximizing people is not thereby justified as a single maximizing individual. Its relevance is to the justification of representative-agent reasoning, rather than to a demonstration that every such approximation fails. The supplied review had no retained article text with which to verify the passage or its full context.

The research identifies Jonathan Hartley’s A Forward-Looking Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu Theorem as an SSRN preprint posted on 1 July 2026. Its reported abstract-level claim is that unrestricted propagation can generate any local Jacobian—the matrix describing local responses in the model. This would concern flexibility in a forward-looking formulation, rather than establish a measured aggregate law. The supplied research describes it as not peer-reviewed; no retained abstract or full text was available to the review to verify the result, assumptions, or publication details.

Donald C. Keenan and Taewon Kim’s Remarks on Stability and the Sonnenschein-Mantel-Debreu Theorem is described as an abstract-only SSRN preprint, not peer-reviewed in the supplied account. The reported argument is that the theorem has limited implications for uniqueness and stability when an economy is modeled through a distribution of consumer demands. This is a proposed qualification concerning modeling and interpretation; the supplied abstract description does not establish empirically validated predictive restrictions. The research metadata lists 9 March 2026 as the date written, 21 March as the posting date, and 25 May as the revision date. The review flags inconsistent treatment of the initial date. Those may be different date categories, but the underlying record was not available to settle the issue.

Evidence limitation: the supplied material reports no prospective empirical demonstration meeting this record’s proposed objective, but it also supplies no bounded search record establishing coverage through 1 November 2026. It therefore does not establish that no such demonstration exists. The research additionally mentions income-dispersion arguments associated with Hildenbrand, while acknowledging that no specific text was reopened; without an identified source and its assumptions, that strand cannot substantiate a particular achievement here. Missing source capture limits verification and is not evidence that the historical results or reported preprint claims are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: define the target market class, goods, equilibrium framework, shocks, and price-adjustment process before testing predictions. State the observable restrictions and how they will be measured in an initial set of markets. Derive uniqueness within the stated domain, local stability under the specified dynamics, and quantitative comparative statics before observing the later outcomes. Make clear which conclusions are mathematical consequences of assumptions and which assumptions have empirical support.
completion_criteria.label: Observable restrictions yield uniqueness, local stability, and quantitative comparative statics

completion_criteria.text: Proposed predictive test: forecast subsequent price and quantity changes using preregistered error bands across several goods and countries. Specify the forecast horizon and compare performance with informative predictive benchmarks, including relevant simpler models. Examine whether the restrictions remain satisfied during the prediction period and report failures as well as successes. A representative-agent fit alone, or a theorem whose assumptions are not measured in the data, would not meet this proposed demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Price and quantity forecasts tested against preregistered bands and benchmarks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: provide enough data, measurement definitions, derivations, and implementation detail for independent replication, subject to any documented access constraints. Seek replication in additional markets and periods, and identify circumstances in which the restrictions or adjustment dynamics fail. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those settings, not literal universality. Claims about large shocks, global convergence, welfare, or policy-regime changes would require separate evidence beyond local stability and successful price and quantity forecasts.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication enabled with documented access constraints and empirical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ECO-02, Prospective transport of causal policy effects across populations, overlaps with testing whether market laws transfer across countries and populations. Its central question is the transport of causal effects; ECO-01 concerns restrictions that permit predictive aggregation and equilibrium analysis. Cross-country success for ECO-01 would not alone establish a general method for transporting policy effects.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-03, A predictive and welfare-coherent theory of boundedly rational choice, concerns the account of individual choice used as an input to aggregation. ECO-01 could potentially use such an account, but improved individual prediction does not automatically solve aggregation. ECO-04, An interpersonally comparable, preference-respecting measure of welfare, addresses comparisons across people that accurate aggregate prices and quantities do not supply. Both remain distinct advances.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-05, Approximately efficient voluntary provision of global public goods, concerns institutions and incentives for collective provision. ECO-06, Household-scale markets for national, occupational, and housing income risk, concerns opportunities to trade and insure particular risks. Aggregate market laws could inform analysis of either, but would not themselves create efficient public-good provision or practical household risk markets.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-07, A verified, manipulable law of sustained productivity growth, seeks a causal basis for changing long-run productive capacity. ECO-01 concerns how household behavior aggregates into market outcomes within a specified framework. Predicting equilibrium responses would not by itself reveal how to generate sustained growth.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-08, Structural counterfactuals for macroeconomic regimes, could use credible aggregation as one ingredient in predicting outcomes under different monetary or policy regimes. It additionally requires modeling institutions, expectations, and responses to regime changes. ECO-09, A general, detail-free allocation compiler for private-information economies, concerns designing allocation mechanisms under informational constraints. ECO-01 could inform predictions of market responses, but would not establish incentive compatibility or a general mechanism-design capability.

Roster-based synthesis: ECO-10, Liquidity and credit without run-prone debt, concerns financial arrangements that supply liquidity and credit while avoiding destabilizing runs. Aggregate market restrictions could inform their analysis, but financial contracts and run dynamics require additional mechanisms. The Cambridge capital controversy, mentioned in the research but not supplied as a separate roster entry, concerns the aggregation of heterogeneous capital goods and is distinct from ECO-01’s demand-aggregation problem.

unresolved_issues: The exact historical theorem statement, assumptions, and qualifications remain unverified against retained source text.
The identities, contents, assumptions, and publication details of the two reported 2026 preprints require source verification.

The Keenan–Kim initial-date concern remains unresolved. The review’s recommendation to present an unexplained date conflict was refined because the supplied metadata explicitly distinguishes date written from date posted; neither date was selected as independently verified.
No bounded search record establishes the state of the field or the objective’s continuing openness as of 1 November 2026.
No specific Hildenbrand source is available to establish which income-dispersion assumptions yield which aggregate restrictions.
The target market class, measurable restrictions, adjustment dynamics, shocks, predictive benchmarks, and acceptable error bands remain to be specified.
It remains unknown whether restrictions strong enough for useful prediction are empirically prevalent and robust to distributional changes, large shocks, or changes in institutions.

brief.title: Reliable market forecasts from household behavior
possible: People planning purchases, production or policy could predict how market prices and quantities would respond to changes in resources or preferences. Those forecasts would build on measurable patterns in what households want and own, with clear limits on which markets they cover.
why: Knowing that households make rational choices does not, by itself, make whole markets predictable. Reliable links between household behavior and market outcomes would give policymakers and economic designers a firmer basis for comparing the consequences of proposed changes.

sources.showed: This handbook chapter reviews mathematical results about total market demand and how it differs from available resources.
sources.cited_for: Individual rationality alone leaves substantial freedom in how total market demand behaves.
sources.not_established: The mathematical result does not identify measurable conditions that reliably predict real markets.

sources.showed: This methodological critique examines whether an economy of individually optimizing people can be treated as a single optimizing person.
sources.cited_for: Treating a whole economy as a single decision-maker needs justification beyond individual rationality.
sources.not_established: The critique does not establish when that approximation predicts observed market responses accurately.

sources.showed: This preprint, which has not been peer reviewed, develops a mathematical argument about flexibility in market models that look ahead.
sources.cited_for: The theoretical barrier may extend to models that incorporate forward-looking behavior.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish measured conditions that yield reliable market forecasts.

sources.who: Donald C. Keenan and Taewon Kim
sources.showed: This preprint, which has not been peer reviewed, examines what the aggregation theorem implies for a market's balance and stability.
sources.cited_for: How consumer differences are modeled may affect conclusions about whether markets settle at a unique balance.
sources.not_established: The argument does not demonstrate predictive conditions measured and tested in real markets.

shown: Debreu's mathematical result, discussed by Shafer and Sonnenschein, shows how widely total demand can vary even when individuals act rationally. Kirman's critique explains why combining such people does not automatically justify modeling the economy as a single decision-maker. These are foundations for the problem; neither supplies a tested market forecasting law.
missing: Researchers still need observable conditions on household preferences, resources or their distribution that meaningfully constrain market behavior.
Models still need to connect those conditions to accurate later forecasts and a price-adjustment process that fits the markets studied.
Independent tests still need to establish where the forecasts work, when the conditions fail and how much uncertainty remains.

milestones.label: Measured conditions determine a stable balance and predictable responses
milestones.explanation: Measured conditions would have to imply a unique equilibrium, where supply meets demand, recovery from small disturbances under stated price adjustments, and numerical responses to changes. This would connect household patterns to market laws.

milestones.label: Later forecasts pass tests set in advance
milestones.explanation: Later price and quantity forecasts across goods and countries would have to meet error bands set in advance and compete with useful benchmarks while the conditions hold. This would test predictive value beyond fitting past data.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and map their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would need enough data and detail, with access limits documented, to repeat tests in further markets and periods and identify failures. This would establish the demonstrated range of the laws.

uncertain: Are conditions strong enough for useful prediction common in real markets?
Would the conditions survive changes in resource distribution, large disturbances or institutions?
Which markets, forecast horizons, comparison models and acceptable error bands should define success?

page.title: Empirical laws of aggregate excess demand
page.definition: Observable restrictions on household preferences, resources and their distribution constrain aggregate excess demand—the amount demanded minus resources available—and predict subsequent market prices and quantities in a specified market class. The restrictions imply a unique equilibrium and local stability under a stated price-adjustment process.

goal.need: United States personal consumption expenditures by households and nonprofit organisations represented 67.9% of GDP in 2024, using the Federal Reserve’s release of 13 March 2025. Demand systems are used to estimate consumption-tax responses and the effects of population composition.

figures.caption: United States economic aggregates in 2024
rows: Household and nonprofit personal consumption expenditures
figures.note: Annual current-dollar totals from the release of 13 March 2025. The consumption share is calculated from these series.

completion.title: An independent prospective field study replicates the model’s price and quantity predictions.
completion.criterion: One independent team prospectively replicates a field study in the same declared market class using new observations. Measured household restrictions must imply a unique equilibrium and local stability under specified price adjustment. Both studies must meet the original protocol’s quantitative endpoint for price and quantity predictions, including lower predictive loss than its specified benchmark. The market, shocks, sample, horizon, scoring rule and error tolerance must be fixed before outcomes. This is a proposed Atlas test; no qualifying combined field demonstration was identified.
completion.set_by: Atlas; no external test combining measured aggregation restrictions, equilibrium properties and prospective field prediction was identified.
completion.basis: Searches of academy and society material and literature using SMD, programme, prize, preregistration, replication and forecast-accuracy terms found no combined endpoint. The stability theorem, fixed-budget sign test and laboratory protocol establish narrower results. Kirman identifies the gap between individual and aggregate maximization. One independently confirmed market class is the narrowest scope consistent with these research objectives.

milestones.title: An exchange economy’s equilibrium is globally stable under the Keenan–Kim distributional bounds.
milestones.criterion: Prove global convergence to equilibrium under dp/dt=z(p) in Keenan–Kim’s smooth continuum exchange model. On its compact trapping price set, require individual excess-demand norms ≤B, demand derivatives with respect to wealth bounded by C, −vᵀS(p)v>ε for v=z(p)/||z(p)||, and directional excess-demand density ≤M relative to uniform spherical measure. S is the aggregate substitution matrix. Rewriting the proof’s bounds gives BCM/√(n−1)<ε as a sufficient condition for n goods. Theorem 1, published on 20 February 2025, establishes conditional stability without measuring these bounds in observed markets.
milestones.set_by: Peer-reviewed proof convention in general-equilibrium theory, instantiated by Keenan and Kim, Global stability in large economies, Theorem 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: Any economy satisfying, assumptions (1)–(4), and having enough goods, will exhibit global stability.

milestones.title: An estimated mean household income-effect matrix is positive definite.
milestones.criterion: Under Härdle–Hildenbrand–Jerison’s household-demand assumptions and metonymy, estimate the mean income-effect matrix A using average derivatives. Metonymy permits cross-sectional comparisons across incomes to identify average income effects. The published sufficient condition is vᵀAv>0 for every nonzero vector v. The 1991 article reports positive-definite estimates from United Kingdom family-expenditure data. This supports a condition for the law of demand with household budgets fixed; it does not establish stability of excess demand with price-dependent wealth.
milestones.set_by: Härdle, Hildenbrand and Jerison, Econometrica, 1991: published sufficient condition and empirical estimation procedure for fixed-budget consumption demand.
milestones.threshold_quote: the mean of all households' income effect matrices be positive definite.

milestones.title: Laboratory markets converge more often to robust equilibria than to fragile equilibria.
milestones.criterion: Apply Crockett–Friedman–Oprea Prediction 5: convergence to revealed competitive equilibrium (RCE) is more frequent in robust than fragile economies. Classification uses earlier individual choices: robust economies have a 25th–75th percentile band of bootstrapped excess demand that does not cross zero outside the RCE price interval. The 2021 study elicited 112 participants’ preferences and traded 16 economies of 12 active traders. Terminal prices were inside predicted intervals in 10/16 economies and allocations inside predicted boxes in 12/16. The goods were two securities paying in different possible states.
milestones.set_by: Crockett, Friedman and Oprea, International Economic Review, 2021, experimental protocol and Prediction 5; the published test concerns laboratory exchange of state-contingent securities.
milestones.threshold_quote: Markets will be less likely to converge to fragile RCE than to robust RCE.

milestones.title: Measured household restrictions predict field prices and quantities in a prospective test.
milestones.criterion: In one declared class of non-laboratory markets, measured household restrictions support a unique equilibrium and local stability under specified price adjustment. Prospective price and quantity forecasts meet a published protocol’s primary accuracy endpoint and have lower predictive loss than its specified benchmark. The protocol fixes shocks, observations, horizon, scoring rule and error tolerance before outcomes. This initial field result supplies the model and test subsequently subjected to independent replication.
milestones.set_by: Atlas: proposed field-validation milestone connecting the published theoretical and laboratory results to the completion test; no external combined milestone was identified.

not_found: No published field-validation protocol was identified that supplies a market class, sample, forecast horizon and numerical error tolerance for the combined endpoint.
The accessible abstract of the 1991 household study does not report household counts or survey years.
The Shafer–Sonnenschein handbook chapter and both supplied SSRN records could not be opened.
